title: One Balcony, Forty Litres Less
script: Narrator: [cheerfully] My balcony garden began with six herb pots and a surprisingly large water bill. Every evening, I poured water until it ran from the containers, assuming that more must be better. Half of it crossed the tiles and disappeared into the drain.
Narrator: A neighbour who grows vegetables suggested an experiment. For two weeks, I would measure what I used, check the soil before watering, and change only one practice at a time.

Narrator: [carefully] During the first week, I used a marked bottle and recorded nearly eighty litres. Some pots were still damp beneath the surface when they received more. The sunniest corner dried quickly, while the shaded pots needed much less.

Narrator: In the second week, I watered early in the morning, grouped plants with similar needs, and added a simple layer of mulch. I also placed trays under appropriate pots, making sure water did not remain stagnant.
Narrator: [surprised] The total fell by about forty litres, and the plants looked no worse. Two herbs actually recovered from yellowing leaves, although I could not prove water was the only reason.
Narrator: The result was encouraging but local. My climate, plant types, and containers shaped the outcome. I would not promise another gardener the same number.

Narrator: [reflective] The most useful change was not a particular product. It was paying attention before acting. I learned to check soil, weather, drainage, and the needs of each plant instead of following one automatic evening routine.

Narrator: I now collect a modest amount of suitable household water when safe, choose plants suited to the space, and review the record each month. Conservation became practical once I could see where the waste occurred.
